title: What are the ways to implement a thread-safe Singleton in Java? Compare eager initialization, synchronized getInstance, double-checked locking with volatile, the Bill Pugh holder idiom, and the enum singleton, and say which is preferred.
keyPoints: Eager: private static final INSTANCE created at class load; thread-safe via JVM class-init guarantee.
Synchronized getInstance: lazy and correct but every call pays the lock cost, a bottleneck under concurrency.
Double-checked locking: volatile field, null check without lock, then lock and re-check; fast after first creation.
Bill Pugh holder: private static inner class holds the instance; lazy, thread-safe, no explicit synchronization.
Enum singleton: simplest and most robust; immune to serialization and reflection attacks.
Preferred: Bill Pugh for lazy loading, enum for the simplest bulletproof version.
If using double-checked locking, the instance field MUST be volatile to prevent seeing a partially constructed object.

s1_definition.oneliner: For a thread-safe Singleton, prefer the Bill Pugh holder idiom for lazy loading or the enum for the simplest bulletproof version.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Eager** – `private static final INSTANCE = new X()`: created at class load, thread-safe for free.
- **Synchronized getInstance** – lazy and correct, but every call acquires the lock.
- **Double-checked locking** – `volatile` field, null check outside lock, re-check inside; fast after creation.
- **Bill Pugh holder** – private static inner class not loaded until first use; lazy, lock-free.
- **Enum singleton** – single instance guaranteed by JVM; serialization-safe, reflection-safe.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has exactly one central vault. No matter how many tellers rush in at the same instant on opening day, there must be only one vault, and it must be fully built before anyone uses it.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Singleton Approaches:

  Eager:           class load ──▶ INSTANCE created ──▶ always available
  Synchronized:    first call ──▶ lock ──▶ create ──▶ every call locks
  Double-checked:  first call ──▶ null? ──▶ lock ──▶ null? ──▶ create
                   later calls ──▶ not null ──▶ return (no lock)
  Bill Pugh:       first call ──▶ loads Holder class ──▶ JVM init lock
                   later calls ──▶ Holder already loaded ──▶ return
  Enum:            class load ──▶ INSTANCE enum constant ──▶ bulletproof
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A thread-safe Singleton must guarantee that only one instance is ever created and all threads see a fully constructed object. The five approaches are eager, synchronized, double-checked locking, Bill Pugh holder, and enum.

I prefer Bill Pugh for lazy loading because it is lazy, fast, and requires no explicit synchronization. For the simplest bulletproof version I use enum, which is also immune to serialization and reflection attacks.

At National Bank of India we use Bill Pugh for the connection pool Singleton and enum for a cached configuration object that gets serialized.

Remember one sentence: prefer the Bill Pugh holder for lazy loading or the enum for the simplest bulletproof Singleton, and if you ever use double-checked locking, the instance field must be volatile.
